area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly a steep, stabilized, slow approach over an obstacle to a chosen spot, touch down within 200 feet of it with little or no float, stop in the shortest safe distance, and go around early when it is not working.
why: Short runways and obstacles leave almost no room for extra speed or height. The landing phase causes more pilot-caused accidents than any other single phase of flight [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]], so precision and a ready go-around matter most here.

warmup: The runway is 2,000 feet long with tall trees at the approach end. The book says you need 1,375 feet to land over a 50-foot obstacle. You are 5 knots fast on short final. Is that a problem? Why?

key_terms.def: Stalling speed in the landing configuration [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
A slow, steep, power-on approach to land in a short space or over obstacles, flown close to minimum controllable airspeed.
The spot you would hit if you never flared. It does not move in the windshield.
A constant-angle glide path to a chosen point at a constant airspeed and configuration.
The difference between the steady wind and the gusts. On a short-field approach add no more than half of it.
The runway left for landing after you clear the obstacle and come down to touchdown.
Braking just short of locking the wheels: they still turn, but reluctantly. This gives the best braking.
Holding the nose up after touchdown so drag helps slow the airplane.
A sudden, drastic change in wind speed and/or direction over a very small area.
Land and Hold Short Operations: landing and stopping before an intersecting runway, taxiway, or set point.

chunks.title: What makes a short-field landing different

body.p: Use short-field procedures when the landing area is short or when obstacles on the approach limit the space you can use. It is a low-speed, power-on approach, flown close to minimum controllable airspeed [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
The goal: precise control of descent rate and airspeed, clear every obstacle, little or no float in the flare, and stop in the shortest possible distance [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

bullets: It is an accuracy approach to an aiming point [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Obstacles present? A slightly steeper approach puts touchdown closer to the obstacle and leaves more room to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Extra speed is the enemy: it can put touchdown too far from the threshold or make the roll longer than the runway [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Your POH short-field procedure, speeds, and flap settings come first. The AFH says the manufacturer's procedures take precedence [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

callout.text: Short field = slow, steep, stable, on the spot, then stop.

check.q: When obstacles are on the approach, why does a slightly steeper approach help?
check.a: It places touchdown closer to the obstacle, which gives more runway to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

chunks.title: Stabilized approach and energy on a steep final

body.p: A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point, flown at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. For short fields the AFH calls it essential, and suggests a wider pattern and longer final (when safe) so you have time to stabilize after you configure and trim [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Pitch and power work together. Small changes in both fix the descent angle and airspeed [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

head: You see
Do this
rows: Too much obstacle clearance; you will land well past the aiming point
Reduce power and lower the nose to steepen the path [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Path will not clear the obstacles safely
Add power and raise the nose to shallow the path [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Doubt about how it will end
Go around, rethink, then try again or divert [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

callout.text: At high angle of attack and low airspeed, raising the nose INCREASES the rate of descent [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Here you are on the back side of the power curve: you need power, not just elevator [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

body.p: AFH stabilized-approach targets for a typical piston airplane: airspeed within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed, bank normally no more than 15 degrees on final, descent rate generally 500-1,000 fpm, and in landing configuration and trim. Not stable by 500 ft above airport elevation in VMC? Go around. Unstable below 300 ft AGL? Go around right away [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. A sink rate over 800-1,000 fpm is excessive; don't dive at the aiming point [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

check.q: You are slow and low on a short-field final. You pull back to stretch it. What happens?
check.a: At high AOA and low speed, more pitch increases the descent rate and can lead to a stall. Add power and raise the nose together, or go around [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and the ACS tolerances)

body.p: Generic AFH procedure. Use your POH speeds and flap settings.

bullets: 1. Before-landing checklist done before base leg [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Pick the aiming point and decide where you will go around.
2. When safe, fly a wider pattern with a longer final to give yourself time to stabilize [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
3. Start final at least 500 feet higher than the touchdown area, usually with the flap setting just before full flaps [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
4. Set pitch and power together for the descent angle and airspeed; trim [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
5. When the field is made: full flaps, lower the nose to hold airspeed, and keep the aiming point still in the windscreen [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
6. Speed: POH speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO if there is none. In gusty air add no more than half the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

7. Over the obstacle you may reduce power slightly, then slowly reduce power [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Never chop it: closing the throttle too fast can cause a sudden sink and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
8. Flare accurately. Touch down at minimum controllable airspeed in about the power-off stall attitude, with little or no float [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
9. Hold the nose up while the elevator works (if the POH recommends it). When the nosewheel touches, apply maximum braking with the yoke held full back [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
10. Keep it straight with rudder, stop, clear the runway, then do the after-landing checklist [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

head: ACS item
Standard
rows: Manufacturer's published approach airspeed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots, with gust factor applied (ACS PA.IV.F.S7)
Within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point, threshold markings, or runway numbers (ACS PA.IV.F.S10)
Proper pitch attitude, no side drift, minimum float, longitudinal axis aligned with and over the centerline (ACS PA.IV.F.S10)
Timely, if the approach cannot be made within these tolerances or is unsafe (ACS PA.IV.F.S12)

callout.text: There is no 'before' allowance: touching down short of the point is outside the standard. Aim to touch ON the point.

check.q: No POH approach speed. VSO is 50 knots. What is the most you should fly on final in calm air?

body.p: The approach is steep and close to stall speed, so judge the flare carefully. Start it late and you fly into the ground; overdo it and you stall early and drop in. Little or no float with good control proves your approach speed was right [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
A little power helps: it blows air over the elevator so you can flare at low speed. A windmilling prop at low airspeed can block that airflow and make the flare hard [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

bullets: Hold the positive pitch after touchdown while the elevator is effective (if the manufacturer recommends it). This is aerodynamic braking [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Nosewheel down: maximum braking right away [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Hold the yoke full back while braking; the airplane tends to lean forward under heavy braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

Best braking is an incipient skid. If the wheels lock, braking drops a lot and tires can be damaged [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. To stop a skid, release brake pressure; pumping the brakes does not help [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
Brakes work better as speed and lift drop [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Make sure your feet are off the brakes at touchdown [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

callout.text: If speed was right and you touched down at minimum control speed, you should not need excessive braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

check.q: What is an 'incipient skid' and why aim for it?
check.a: Brake pressure just short of locking the wheels; they still turn but reluctantly. It gives the best braking; a locked wheel brakes much worse [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

chunks.title: Wind, density altitude, weight, and the runway surface

body.p: Before you pick a runway, compare the landing distance you need with the runway you have [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Many things make that distance grow.

head: Factor
Effect on landing distance
rows: Same IAS but higher TAS. At 5,000 feet, about 16% longer than at sea level (about 3.5% per 1,000 feet) [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Each 10 ft above 50 ft over the threshold
About 10% longer; uphill shortens the roll [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.7]] [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]]

body.p: Worked example from this Cessna 172R chart: 2,000 feet pressure altitude, 20 degrees C, zero wind. Total to clear a 50-foot obstacle = 1,375 feet; ground roll = 605 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

bullets: 4-knot tailwind: the note says add 10% for each 2 knots, so +20%: 1,375 x 1.20 = 1,650 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].
Dry grass: add 45% of the ground roll: 0.45 x 605 = about 272 feet, so about 1,647 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].
AC 91-79B adds a safety margin of at least 15% to book landing distance: 1,375 x 1.15 = about 1,581 feet [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.8.1]].

body.p: Wet runways: water cuts tire friction and braking. Hydroplaning tires ride on water, so braking and steering are almost nil. Minimum hydroplaning speed is about 9 x the square root of tire pressure; 36 psi gives 54 knots. Landing faster than recommended raises the risk. Land into the wind, avoid abrupt inputs, and use aerodynamic braking fully [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]] [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

callout.text: Tailwind plus a slippery runway is worse than either alone: more groundspeed at touchdown and more float [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]].

check.q: Book total distance is 1,310 feet. You have a 6-knot tailwind (chart note: +10% per 2 knots). What do you need?

body.p: Two methods: crab and wing-low (sideslip). The AFH recommends wing-low in most cases; you should know both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Wing-low keeps the ground track and nose on the centerline all the way through touchdown and rollout [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

bullets: Wing-low: rudder to line up the nose with the runway; aileron into the wind just enough to stop the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
Crab: hold the crab angle, then use rudder to line up the nose just before touchdown. Too early or too late gives a side load [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
Keep the upwind wing down in the flare. As speed drops, add more aileron and rudder [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Touch down on the upwind main wheel first [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Rollout: more and more aileron into the wind; full aileron into the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
With rudder-linked nosewheel steering, relax rudder as the nosewheel touches to avoid a swerve [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

body.p: Limits: if full opposite rudder cannot stop the turn, the wind is too strong for that runway; land on a better runway or another airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. The AFH says airplanes are flight tested to be controllable in 90-degree crosswinds up to 0.2 VSO, with the demonstrated value on a placard (airplanes certificated after May 3, 1962) [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. Today's Part 23 is performance-based and no longer lists that number [[60:102|14 CFR 23.2135]], so use the demonstrated crosswind in your POH.

callout.text: Side loads from drifting can tip a tricycle-gear airplane. You can fight a roll-over with ailerons, rudder, or nosewheel steering, but NOT brakes [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]. On wet runways, crosswind also cuts braking [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.10]]. So heavy short-field braking and a strong crosswind are a risky mix.

check.q: Wing-low method: which wheel touches first?

chunks.title: Gusts, wind shear, and wake turbulence

body.p: Gusts: add no more than half the gust factor on a short-field approach [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Example from the AFH: 70 knots normal, gusts of 15 knots, fly 77 knots [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Remember extra speed means a longer landing.

Wind shear: a headwind turning into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On a short-field approach you are already slow, so there is little margin. A microburst on approach can force the airplane to the ground short of the runway; downdrafts can reach 6,000 fpm [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Watch for heavy rain shafts, virga, or a ring of blowing dust [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

A big, sudden airspeed gain near storms may be the start of a microburst and a reason to stop the approach; but microbursts are often lopsided, so don't count on that warning [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Don't cut power and lower the nose for the gain; that leaves you nose-low and power-low when the tailwind hits [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. Go around at the first sign; some microbursts can't be escaped with any known technique [[28:266|AWH 22-11]].

Wake turbulence: vortices exist from rotation to touchdown and sink several hundred feet per minute. Near the ground (within 100-200 feet) they drift sideways at 2-3 knots [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. A light quartering tailwind can push them into the touchdown zone and needs maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

head: Landing behind a larger aircraft that is...
AIM procedure
rows: Stay at or above its path; land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Land well before its rotation point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Doing a low approach, missed approach, or touch-and-go

callout.text: Short-field conflict: you want to touch down near the threshold, but behind a landing heavy you must land past its touchdown point. If that leaves too little runway, don't land: extend, ask the tower for spacing, or use another runway. The pilot must adjust to avoid wake encounters, warning or not [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

check.q: A larger airplane just departed from your short runway. Where do you plan to touch down?
check.a: Well before its rotation point, where its wake begins [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

body.p: Plan the go-around before you start final. A go-around is a normal maneuver, not a failure. It is dangerous only when late or done wrong. Delay comes from landing expectancy ('it will work out') and pride [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

bullets: Power: full (or max allowable) power, smoothly and right away; carb heat off if applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Attitude: you are trimmed for low speed, so expect strong nose-up and left yaw. Use forward pressure and right rudder; don't pitch up without airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Configuration: once the descent stops, take flaps to the POH go-around/takeoff setting, then the rest in small steps. Dumping full flaps at once can make you settle into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Ground effect: don't try to climb out of it too early [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: Short-field go-around trigger points: you can't hold the speed, you will not touch down within 200 feet of the point, you float, or you drift. For floating, the AFH says go around if a landing cannot be made on the first third of the runway or the airplane drifts sideways [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. On a short field your 200-foot touchdown limit usually comes first.

LAHSO: students and pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate. The PIC may accept or decline, and should accept only after determining the airplane can safely land and stop within the published Available Landing Distance (ALD) [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Pilots should get a LAHSO clearance only with at least a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility. Read it back with the words 'HOLD SHORT OF (runway/taxiway/point)'. A LAHSO clearance does not stop you from going around [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

callout.text: If you can't safely stop before the hold-short point, say so early: tell ATC you want the full length or another runway, ideally before the clearance is issued [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

check.q: What are the three go-around principles, in order?

chunks.title: Traffic, radios, right runway, and low-altitude traps

body.p: Collision hazards. At a non-towered airport, monitor and talk on CTAF within 10 miles. Use pattern calls such as 'On left base for runway [XX]' [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]] [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]] [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. Avoid 'to' and 'for' when they could be mistaken for numbers [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.3]]. A wider pattern and longer final is non-standard for others, so say where you are. Keep scanning for blind spots; high wings block the view above [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.113(g): aircraft on final or landing have right-of-way, but the lower aircraft may not cut in front of or overtake one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]].

body.p: Right runway: check the runway number and alignment on every final; study the airport diagram ahead of time. If in doubt, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. Scan the runway and its ends for traffic, vehicles, and obstructions before you commit.

Low-altitude stall/spin and CFIT: the approach is slow and steep over obstacles. Don't fix a low final with pitch alone or by pulling up flaps [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. Don't skid the base-to-final turn; an overshoot means go around, and be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees there [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A go-around at high pitch, high power, and low speed is a classic stall/spin setup if rudder is wrong [[13:12|AC 61-67C para 109]]. CFIT is a top cause of GA fatal accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

Distractions: do checklists early so you can watch traffic and fly [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Task saturation leads to fixation; stop, think, slow down, and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Keep a hand on the throttle on approach [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

Runway incursions: after landing, get the whole airplane, tail included, past the hold short line. Don't change frequencies or move flaps and trim until clear of all runways. Don't accept a last-minute turnoff you are not sure you can make [[7:7|AC 91-73B]].

check.q: After landing, when should you raise the flaps and switch to ground?
check.a: Only after the whole airplane is clear of all runways, past the hold short line [[7:7|AC 91-73B]].

body.p: The AFH lists these short-field errors [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]:

head: Error
Fix
rows: Final so steep it needs a high sink rate
Better base placement; stabilize early; go around if sink is over 800-1,000 fpm [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Correct early with pitch and power together [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Too slow: can't flare, hard landing
Add power early; go around if slow and low [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Hold the speed; go around if you will miss the point [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Power to idle too early in the flare
Touch down at minimum controllable airspeed [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]
Brake to an incipient skid, not a lock [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Rudder and aileron into the wind; not brakes alone [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]

check.q: What does the AFH say happens if you close the throttle too fast in the short-field flare?
check.a: An immediate increase in the descent rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

scenario.title: Hot afternoon, short strip, trees
scenario.setup: You fly a 172R to a non-towered airport at 2,000 feet pressure altitude, 20 C. Runway 34 is 2,000 feet, paved, with 50-foot trees before the threshold. Runway 16 has no trees. The wind was calm, but a new AWOS says 200 at 10 gusting 20. A twin is doing a touch-and-go on 34 ahead of you. There are dark rain shafts 10 miles west. Your passenger keeps asking questions on downwind.

questions.q: Can you land on runway 34 by the book?
questions.a: The chart gives 1,375 feet over a 50-foot obstacle in zero wind [[1:456|PHAK A-4]]. With a 15% margin about 1,581 feet [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.8.1]]. It fits 2,000 feet, but only with on-speed, on-spot flying. Any extra speed or height eats the margin fast [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]] [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

questions.q: Which runway does the new wind favor, and what does that do?
questions.a: 200 degrees is 40 degrees off runway 16, so 16 now has a headwind and no trees: pick 16. Runway 34 would have a tailwind and a crosswind. A tailwind adds about 21% for 10 knots [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Gusts: add no more than half the gust factor, which also adds distance [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Check the crosswind against the demonstrated value [[24:190|AFH 9-19]].

Its wake may linger on the runway, especially with a light quartering tailwind. Wait at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Extend your downwind and tell traffic on CTAF [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

questions.q: The rain shafts are moving closer. What is the risk on a slow, short-field final?
questions.a: Possible microburst: a headwind that turns to a tailwind and downdrafts can force you to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. If it moves in, hold off or divert.

questions.q: On short final over the trees you are low and slow and the passenger is talking. What do you do?
questions.a: Ask for quiet; fly first [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Don't pull the nose up to stretch it; that raises the sink rate near the stall [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Add power, or go around right away: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist before base and the after-landing checklist once clear of the runway.
skills.practice: Do the checklist at the same pattern point every time; say it out loud.

skills.do: Make CTAF pattern calls (or tower calls), including a call for a wide pattern or long final.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the calls: downwind, base, final, clear of the runway.

skills.do: Line up with the correct or assigned runway.
skills.practice: On every final, say the runway number you see and compare it with your plan or clearance.

skills.do: Scan the runway and nearby area for traffic and obstructions.
skills.practice: Look at both ends of the runway and the final path before turning base and again on final.

skills.do: Pick a touchdown point considering wind, surface, and obstacles, and aim for it.
skills.practice: Before each landing, name the point (for example, the first stripe after the numbers) and check where you actually touched.

skills.do: Set the POH short-field configuration, speed, and trim, and keep a stabilized approach with pitch and power.
skills.practice: Fly long finals first; then shorten them as your corrections get smaller.

skills.do: Hold the POH approach speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots with gust factor applied.
skills.practice: Call out the speed every few seconds on final; your CFI notes every deviation.

skills.do: Keep directional control and crosswind correction all the way through rollout.
skills.practice: Practice wing-low on crosswind days with your CFI; fly the length of the runway in a sideslip just above it.

skills.do: Use smooth, timely control inputs before, during, and after touchdown.
skills.practice: Reduce power slowly in the flare; keep the yoke coming back as you settle.

skills.do: Touch down within 200 feet beyond or on the point, no drift, minimum float, aligned on centerline.
skills.practice: Use runway markers or stripes to measure your touchdown; log the distance each time.

skills.do: Use the POH configuration and braking: maximum braking without locking the wheels.
skills.practice: On a long runway, practice firm braking with the yoke full back until it feels natural.

skills.do: Go around on time if out of tolerance or unsafe.
skills.practice: Pre-brief your triggers; your CFI calls surprise go-arounds on short final.

skills.do: Use runway incursion avoidance after landing.
skills.practice: Brief the exit taxiway before landing; stop past the hold short line before cleanup.

quiz.q: With no manufacturer's approach speed, what speed does the AFH use for a short-field approach?
options: Not more than 1.1 VSO
1.5 VSO
1.4 VSO
Not more than 1.3 VSO

quiz.q: Your approach speed is 61 knots and the gust factor is 12 knots. What is the most the AFH says to add?
options: 0 knots
12 knots
6 knots
15 knots
quiz.why: In gusty air no more than one-half the gust factor is added: 12 / 2 = 6 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

quiz.q: The AFH says a short-field final generally starts at least how high above the touchdown area?
options: 500 feet
300 feet
800 feet
1,000 feet
quiz.why: At least 500 feet higher than the touchdown area [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

quiz.q: Obstacle clearance looks excessive and you will touch down well past the aiming point. What do you do?
options: Reduce power and lower the nose
Add power and raise the nose to stretch the glide to the aiming point
Raise the nose and hold the same power setting
Retract some flaps and hold the same pitch
quiz.why: Reduce power while lowering the pitch to steepen the path [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

quiz.q: At high angle of attack and low airspeed, increasing pitch attitude will:
options: Decrease the descent rate
Not change the descent rate
Increase the descent rate
Increase airspeed
quiz.why: At high AOA and low airspeed, more pitch increases the rate of descent [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

quiz.q: ACS touchdown standard for a short-field landing:
options: Within 200 feet beyond or on the point
Within 200 feet before or after the point
Within 400 feet beyond the point
In the first third of the runway
quiz.why: Touch down within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point, threshold markings, or runway numbers (ACS PA.IV.F.S10).

quiz.q: About how much does a 10-knot tailwind increase landing distance?
quiz.why: A tail wind of ten knots increases landing distance by about 21 percent [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

quiz.q: A student pilot is offered a LAHSO clearance. The AIM says:
options: Accept it if the runway looks long enough
Accept it, then go around if needed
Accept only at night
Students should not participate in LAHSO
quiz.why: Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

quiz.q: On a short-field approach near rain showers, airspeed suddenly jumps 15 knots. What does the AWH say?
options: Good news: reduce power and lower the nose to get back on speed right away
It may mean an airspeed loss is coming; it may be reason to stop the approach
Ignore it; only airspeed losses matter, and an increase never leads to a loss
Add flaps to use up the extra speed and keep the same power setting
quiz.why: A rapid or large airspeed increase near convective weather may signal a coming decrease and may be reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]]. Cutting power and lowering the nose leaves you nose-low, power-low when the tailwind hits [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

takeaways: Slow, steep, stable: POH speed or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus no more than half the gust factor.
Fix the path with pitch and power together; at low speed, pulling up makes you sink faster.
Touch down on the point (up to 200 feet beyond) with little or no float, then brake hard without locking the wheels.
Tailwind, extra speed, weight, altitude, slope, and wet or grass surfaces all add distance; run the numbers first.
Behind bigger airplanes, land clear of the wake even if it costs runway; if it won't fit, don't land there.
Brief your go-around triggers before final and act on them early: power, attitude, configuration.
cfi_notes: Have the student name the aiming point and the go-around triggers on downwind; examiners often watch for that briefing.
Common: students fly fast 'for safety' and float well past the point. Show the 172R chart math so they see what 5 knots costs.
Common: chopping power over the obstacle and dropping in. Teach slow, gradual power reduction (AFH 9-22).
Practice first on a long runway with an imaginary obstacle and a marked spot; measure touchdown error every time.
Brief the short-field vs. wake conflict (land past the heavy's touchdown point vs. land near the threshold) as an ADM exercise.
Watch base-to-final turns on a wider pattern: tailwind on base can tempt a skid. Overshoot = go around (AFH 5-20).
Teach go-arounds from full flaps at low speed: strong nose-up and left yaw; flaps up in steps (AFH 9-11).
gaps: Airplane-specific short-field speeds, flap settings, power use, braking and flap-retraction technique, landing distance charts, and demonstrated crosswind are in the POH/AFM, not these resources. The 172R chart is only an example.
AC 91-79B rules of thumb (height over threshold, slope, 15% margin) are written for operators' landing assessments; they are used here as general guidance.

FAA cancelled AC 00-54 (Pilot Wind Shear Guide, still named in the PHAK) in 2022; wind shear guidance now sits in the Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28B). The AWH covers microburst clues, approach encounters and the general rule to hold pitch and accept lower airspeed [[28:268|AWH 22-13]], but its encounter studies are airline-style (crews, thrust, stick shaker) and it gives no step-by-step escape procedure for small airplanes. Use the POH/AFM and your CFI.
No dedicated CFIT-on-short-field-approach section was found; covered through obstacle clearance, low-final corrections, and RMH accident causes.
How the examiner specifies the touchdown point is not described in these resources.
Towered-airport landing phraseology beyond the LAHSO readback is not covered in the pages used.

activities.title: Steepen, shallow, or go around?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.
buckets: Steepen: less power, lower the nose
Shallow: more power, raise the nose

items.t: Obstacle clearance looks much more than you need
You will touch down well past the aiming point
The aiming point moves down, away from the horizon
Your path will not safely clear the trees
The aiming point moves up toward the horizon
Still not stabilized at 500 feet above the airport in VMC
The approach becomes unstable below 300 feet AGL
You have doubts about how the approach will end

activities.title: Fly the short-field landing in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Finish the before-landing checklist before base leg
Start final at least 500 feet above the touchdown area, often with the flap setting just before full
When the field is made, set full flaps and lower the nose to hold airspeed
Over the obstacle, ease the power back slowly; never chop it
Touch down at minimum controllable airspeed, with little or no float
After touchdown, hold the nose up while the elevator still works (if the POH recommends it)
Nosewheel down: maximum braking with the yoke held full back
Clear the runway, then do the after-landing checklist

activities.title: What does it cost in runway?
activities.intro: Tap a condition, then how much longer the landing gets.

pairs.r: 5% faster landing speed and 10% more distance
About 16% more than at sea level
About 400 feet more than crossing at 50 feet

activities.title: True or false: go-arounds, wake, and LAHSO

cards.s: When you add full power to go around, expect the nose to rise and the airplane to yaw left.
cards.why: Yes. You are trimmed for low speed, so hold forward pressure and add right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: If you have to go around, it means you flew a bad approach.
cards.why: No. Any approach may end in a go-around. The AFH calls the idea that a go-around always means a poor approach a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: Once the descent stops in a go-around, raise all the flaps at once.
cards.why: No. Raise them in small steps. Raising them all at once can cost lift and let you settle into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: After a larger airplane does a touch-and-go on your runway, wait at least 2 minutes before you land.
cards.why: Yes. Its vortices can settle and drift along the runway, so the AIM asks for at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

cards.s: Once you accept a LAHSO clearance, you may not go around.
cards.why: No. A LAHSO clearance does not rule out a rejected landing. Keep clear of other traffic and tell the controller right away [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

cards.s: When you read back a LAHSO clearance, include the words "hold short of" and the runway, taxiway, or point.
cards.why: Yes. Controllers need a full read back of every LAHSO clearance [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH lists no short-field approach speed. VSO is 40 knots. The wind is down the runway at 10 knots, gusting 22. Using the AFH guidance, what is the most you should fly on final?
options: 52 knots
70 knots
64 knots
58 knots
final_quiz.why: Not more than 1.3 VSO: 1.3 x 40 = 52 knots. The gust factor is 22 - 10 = 12 knots; add no more than half, 6 knots: 52 + 6 = 58 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

final_quiz.q: On a checkride in smooth air, your POH short-field approach speed is 62 KIAS. Which airspeed on final would be outside the ACS standard?
options: 56 KIAS
70 KIAS
60 KIAS
66 KIAS
final_quiz.why: The ACS allows the published speed +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.F.S7): 62 - 5 = 57 and 62 + 10 = 72 KIAS. 56 is below 57. The AFH uses the same +10/-5 window for a stabilized approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: You are on speed on a short-field final, but you can see the path will not safely clear the trees ahead. What should you do?
options: Raise the nose without adding power
Add power and raise the nose together
Raise the flaps one notch
Reduce power and lower the nose
final_quiz.why: Add power while raising the pitch to make the path shallower [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Pitch alone at low speed makes you sink faster, and raising the flaps makes you sink more [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH say a small amount of power can help in the short-field flare?
options: It sends more air over the elevator, so it works better at low speed
It lets you float longer so you can pick a spot and ease onto the runway
It keeps the stall warning horn quiet so you can concentrate on the touchdown
It makes the wheel brakes work better by pressing the tires onto the runway
final_quiz.why: A little power gives the elevator more airflow and more authority at low airspeed. A windmilling propeller at low speed can block that airflow and make the flare hard [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

final_quiz.q: On a 2,000-foot runway you float in the flare. You can see you will touch down about 400 feet past your chosen point. What is the best action?
options: Push the nose down to force the wheels on
Pull back harder to stop the float
Go around
Keep floating, then brake extra hard
final_quiz.why: Touching down 400 feet past the point is outside the 200-foot standard (ACS PA.IV.F.S10), so go around in time (ACS PA.IV.F.S12). Long floats use up runway and should be avoided on short runways [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]. Pushing the nose down near the runway can put the nosewheel down first [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].

final_quiz.q: Your nosewheel is now on the runway after a short-field touchdown. Which braking gives the shortest safe stop?
options: Pump the brakes hard in short bursts, with the yoke held neutral
Lock the wheels and hold them locked, with the yoke held full back for the shortest stop
Maximum braking with the yoke full back, just short of locking the wheels
Light braking with forward yoke to load the nosewheel and keep the tires from skidding
final_quiz.why: Apply maximum braking with the yoke held full back. Best braking is an incipient skid: the wheels still turn, but reluctantly. A locked wheel brakes much worse and can damage the tire [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

final_quiz.q: Use the Cessna 172R chart. Pressure altitude is 4,000 feet, temperature 10 C, and you have a 9-knot headwind. About how much total distance do you need to land over a 50-foot obstacle?
options: About 1,132 feet
1,415 feet
About 1,557 feet
About 1,274 feet
final_quiz.why: The chart gives 1,415 feet at 4,000 feet and 10 C. Note 2 says decrease 10% for each 9 knots of headwind: 1,415 x 0.90 = about 1,274 feet [[1:456|PHAK A-4]].

final_quiz.q: You land at an airport 5,000 feet above sea level. Why is your landing distance longer than at sea level?
options: You must fly a higher indicated airspeed on final to keep the same margin
The brakes create less stopping force in thin air, so the ground roll gets longer
Same indicated airspeed, but a higher true airspeed at touchdown
Flaps do not work above 3,000 feet, so you must land with less flap
final_quiz.why: You land at the same IAS, but thinner air means a higher TAS. Braking and drag stay the same, so the extra distance comes from the higher TAS: about 16% longer at 5,000 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

final_quiz.q: You must land on a short, wet runway. What does the PHAK advise?
options: Land a little faster than normal for better control and a shorter ground roll
Choose a runway with a tailwind so you touch down sooner and use less runway
Brake hard right at touchdown, even if the wheels lock, to stop in the shortest distance
Land into the wind, avoid abrupt inputs, and use aerodynamic braking fully
final_quiz.why: Landing faster raises the risk of hydroplaning. Land into the wind, avoid abrupt control inputs, expect braking problems, and use aerodynamic braking to its fullest [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

final_quiz.q: You touch down drifting in a crosswind on a short runway, and one main wheel starts to lift off. What does the AFH say will NOT help prevent a roll-over?
options: Ailerons
Brakes
Rudder
Nosewheel steering
final_quiz.why: Touching down while drifting puts a side load on the tires that can roll a tricycle-gear airplane over. Below the roll-over angle you can fight it with ailerons, rudder, or nosewheel steering, but not brakes [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

final_quiz.q: A larger airplane lands ahead of you on your short runway and touches down well past the threshold. Your short-field distance needs most of the runway. What should you plan?
options: Fly below its path so you can touch down near the threshold and stay clear of it
Stay at or above its path, and land past its touchdown point or go around
Wait 30 seconds, then land near the threshold, since its wake will have settled by then
Land at the threshold right away, before its wake has time to spread across the runway
final_quiz.why: Stay at or above the larger airplane's path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Its wake ends where it touched down, so the area before that point may hold its vortices [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]] [[34:149|AIM 7-4-4]]. If too little runway is left past that point, go around and decide whether to try again or divert [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

final_quiz.q: You are planning a short-field approach near a thunderstorm. Which clue may warn of a microburst?
options: Light morning ground fog over the airport and a calm wind at the surface
A steady wind straight down the runway, with no change in speed or direction
High, thin cirrus clouds well away from the storm and no rain below them
Virga at cloud base and a ring of blowing dust on the ground
final_quiz.why: An intense rain shaft, virga at cloud base, and a ring of blowing dust can mark a microburst. On approach it can force the airplane to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

final_quiz.q: You start a go-around at low speed with full flaps. You add full power, and the nose starts to pitch up hard. What should you do?
options: Let the nose rise to climb away from the ground quickly and keep the flaps full down
Hold forward pressure and right rudder, and don't pitch up until you have airspeed
Raise all the flaps right away to reduce drag and stop the nose from rising
Reduce power until the nose comes down, then add power again slowly
final_quiz.why: You are trimmed for low speed, so full power raises the nose and yaws the airplane left. Use forward pressure and right rudder. Letting the nose rise too early at low altitude can cause a stall [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
